name: River West
label: River West
about_prose: River West sits on the west bank of the Deschutes River, directly across from downtown Bend, in the grid of streets between NW Newport Avenue and the river trail. Ponderosa pines shade most blocks, and the streets are narrow enough that traffic moves slowly even before you reach a stop sign. A resident can walk to a full grocery store, a dozen restaurants, and the river within the same ten minutes it takes to drive to the far side of town. That combination of river frontage and a walkable commercial strip is the reason people choose this neighborhood over Bend's newer subdivisions on the edges of the city, and it comes with a real cost, described below.

The neighborhood's history is tied to Bend's lumber-mill economy. The Shevlin-Hixon Lumber Company built a mill on the Deschutes River in 1916, one of two mills, with Brooks-Scanlon on the opposite bank, that helped drive Bend's population from 536 in the 1910 census to 5,415 in 1920 and 8,848 in 1930. Shevlin-Hixon sold its operation to Brooks-Scanlon in 1950 as the old-growth pine ran out, and the combined mills shut down in the early 1950s. Much of River West's original housing, small Craftsman bungalows and cottages on narrow lots, dates to that boom period. Oregon's 2019 middle housing law, House Bill 2001, now requires cities including Bend to allow duplexes through quadplexes on residential lots, which is part of why the original bungalow stock now sits next to newer duplexes and other infill construction.

NW Newport and NW Galveston Avenues carry the neighborhood's commercial life. Newport Avenue Market, an employee-owned grocery store at 1121 NW Newport Ave, opened on the westside in the early 1990s. A few blocks over, 10 Barrel Brewing's westside pub sits at 1135 NW Galveston Ave near Spork, Zydeco Kitchen and Cocktails, and Dump City Dumplings. All of it is walkable from inside the neighborhood, which is the appeal and, increasingly, the friction. Growth along the Galveston corridor since the pandemic has pushed diners and shoppers onto residential side streets, and neighbors have told local reporters they post signs near their mailboxes to keep cars from blocking mail delivery. A 2025 redevelopment on Galveston is removing 16 existing parking spaces as part of its plan, and the city's response so far has been wider bike lanes and a raised crosswalk rather than added parking. A buyer within a block or two of Newport or Galveston should plan on competing for curb space on weekend nights.

River access does not require a car. Drake Park, 13 acres on Mirror Pond established by the city in 1921, forms the neighborhood's eastern edge and is open daily from 5 a.m. to 10 p.m. The Deschutes River Trail's Pioneer Reach segment runs south from there, a 1.7-mile mix of paved path, gravel, and sidewalk connecting Drake Park to McKay Park, Miller's Landing, and Pioneer Park, with a boardwalk under the Newport Avenue bridge rebuilt in 2022 and 2023. Pageant Park, a 0.3-acre riverfront park at 691 NW Drake Road acquired by the parks district in 1977, is named for the Bend Water Pageant, a Fourth of July river festival that ran from 1933 to 1965 and drew more than 18,000 visitors to its 1940 event, nearly doubling the town's population of roughly 10,000 for the weekend. About a mile south, the Bend Whitewater Park opened in September 2015 with a three-channel stretch of river for tubing, kayaking, and paddleboarding, just before the trail reaches the Old Mill District, the 270-acre redevelopment of the old lumber-mill site.

The River West Neighborhood Association was recognized by Bend City Council on April 17, 2002, one of the city's 13 neighborhood districts, and it is the body residents go through to weigh in on the development pressure described above. Kids in the neighborhood attend Highland School at Kenwood, a K-5 campus at 701 NW Newport Ave inside the neighborhood boundary that feeds into Cascade Middle School and Summit High School. Walking distance to an elementary school, a commercial strip, and the river trail suits a buyer who wants a car-optional routine more than someone who wants a quiet street with no foot traffic. The lots are old and small by Bend standards, the streets are narrow, and the parking conflict on Galveston has no resolution yet. In exchange, a resident gets about as close to downtown Bend and the river as it is possible to live, on foot in either direction.

amenities.name: Drake Park and Mirror Pond
amenities.description: A 13-acre park at 777 NW Riverside Blvd with nearly half a mile of riverfront, open lawn, an outdoor stage, and a river float take-out, on the neighborhood's eastern boundary.

amenities.name: Pageant Park
amenities.description: A 0.3-acre park at 691 NW Drake Road on the Deschutes River Trail, with riverfront lawn, benches, and a small boat launch.
amenities.access: Pedestrian bridge connects to Drake Park

amenities.name: Deschutes River Trail (Pioneer Reach)
amenities.description: A paved multi-use trail widened in 2023, connecting Drake Park north to Pacific Park and south to the Old Mill District, with footbridges crossing the river.

amenities.name: Bend Whitewater Park
amenities.description: A whitewater park opened September 2015 at 166 SW Shevlin Hixon Dr, with a three-channel river stretch for tubing, kayaking, and paddleboarding, about half a mile south along the river.

amenities.name: Highland School at Kenwood Elementary
amenities.description: A K-5 Bend-La Pine campus at 701 NW Newport Ave within the neighborhood, feeding to Cascade Middle and Summit High.
amenities.access: Walkable from most River West addresses

amenities.name: Old Mill District
amenities.description: A 270-acre mixed-use redevelopment of the former lumber-mill site, with 60-plus shops and restaurants and the Hayden Homes Amphitheater, about a mile south along the river.
amenities.access: Via the Deschutes River Trail or a 5-minute drive
